title: Where do people typically draw the line for what counts as AI game dev?
author: Talryath
selftext:
I'm not confused when this comes to pure prompt development. But when someone generates a length of code to be quicker with development, is capable of reading it over, understanding it, and even making adjustments to better fit their design--including replacing whole sections/functions because the AI went a route that the dev recognizes would be a pain later on--is the game still labeled as AI developed?   
Crimson Desert said they included some AI in their DLC but as placeholders that will be removed upon development, so are they considered AI developed?  
This all is so new so there probably is no stable answer yet, but I just want to get a better idea of where people draw the line when using AI tools in game development.  
If there is another post like this please direct me to it..

comments.author: hippieman
comments.body: If you are not hand writing 1s and 0s by hand its AI.

replies.author: wadrasil
replies.body: The compiler writes most of my goofy expressions into actual code as well.

comments.author: MilaKunisWatermelon
comments.body:
Depends which people.

If you mean Reddit, they don’t draw the line and you’re evil just for not leading a protest against AI.

If you mean kids that are actually likely to buy games, they don’t care at all how a game is made so long as it’s fun.

comments.author: Relevant-Positive-48
comments.body:
If you're using LLM coding assistance that didn't exist before generative AI became a thing then you're doing AI game development -> but I'm fairly sure that's not what you're actually asking.

What you're highlighting is the difference between someone using AI who understands the output and can, if necessary, take over and someone using AI who doesn't understand the output and, at some level, needs to accept what the AI gives them -> but I don't even think that's what you're actually curious about.

What I think you're actually wondering is whether or not the people who attack AI generated/assisted games would be mollified by someone using AI who knows what they're doing.  The answer to that is no.  There's no mollifying those determined to attack AI in any way shape or form that it's used.  My suggestion is to focus on making your game and not worry about them.

comments.author: egonosz
comments.body:
I mean if you use in anyway ai through development, I guess it would be “ai gamedev”.

However if someone writes a 3 line prompt and a ai would make from it software, I wouldn’t call that software game and the person game dev.

However, you just need to disclose that what the platforms tell you to disclose.

comments.author: AistoB
comments.body: I’m purely a hobbyist just having fun right now, but I suppose it’s the user facing part that people have the strongest reaction to currently. Artwork, animation and music. I feel that this will change in time as we realign to the only true metric, is it fun?

comments.author: Pkittens
comments.body:
there are 2 anti-AI positions:          
\- literally any use of AI is morally reprehensible no matter what         
\- if you can tell it's AI then it's bad because it looks cheap

comments.author: M4xs0n
comments.body: If you use AI for literally anything you will be hated. So just use everything and have no regret

comments.author: re-skob
comments.body: If you're still reading lines of code yngmi

comments.author: YesImYou
comments.body: It depends; for some people, just googling something and reading the gemini result makes you an AI game dev, for others generating a full game in one prompt makes you an AI game dev. The truth is there is no "line"

comments.author: Baalzeg
comments.body:
AI Assisted ≠ AI made

Aún así, da enteramente igual. Lo que cuenta es la idea.

comments.author: Turbulent-Armadillo9
comments.body: Man… when I’m done with the game I don’t want to put that disclosure up… I also don’t want to redraw everything just cuz. My art is like 50/50 right now.

comments.author: shaymagen
comments.body: For me the line is whether you can own the result. If you can read the code, change the bits that fight your design, and ship something you’d defend in a postmortem, I’m fine calling it AI-assisted rather than “AI made.” Pure prompt-and-pray is a different bucket. Crimson Desert using temp AI placeholders that get replaced feels closer to a production tool than to an AI-developed game.
